newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: FEATURE - Foreign banks flock to Argentina.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Foreign banks flock to Argentina.

text.p: Stroll down Buenos Aires' bustling Callao Avenue these days and it is not the old-world cafes that catch your eye but the facades of foreign banks trying to cash in on Argentina's banking revolution.
Downtown in "La City", as yuppies call their financial centre, you may not see a single local bank for blocks.
Overseas financial institutions are flocking here, lured by expanding capital markets, rising domestic savings rates and restructuring in the banking industry.

A string of recent acquisitions in Argentina by foreign institutions shows that overseas banks and brokerages already here are increasing their presence and those not present are thinking of setting up shop.

The U.S. brokerage house Merrill Lynch, already operating in Argentina, has bought a seat on the Buenos Aires Stock Exchange and hopes to start trading directly there this month, Merrill's local president Guillermo Reca told Reuters.
"We think the local market will develop in the mid term, and we want to take part in that development," Reca said.
According to market sources, the U.S. brokerage Smith Barney is also considering establishing itself in Buenos Aires.
Early last month, Spain's Banco Bilbao Vizcaya reached agreement to buy 30 percent of the stock of local bank Banco Frances del Rio de la Plata SA.

Spain's Banco Santander has expanded its pension fund operations here, after pension fund Origenes AFJP jointly owned by Santander and Banco de la Provincia de Buenos Aires bought fund manager's Activa-Anticipar for $100 million.

Adalberto Zelmar Barbosa, executive director of ABRA, which represents the interests of 60 foreign banks, told Reuters he receives many inquiries from overseas institutions. He said two Brazilian banks are looking to set up in Buenos Aires, Dutch bank Rabobank has made inquiries and ABN Amro, which is already here, is expanding.
REASONS BEHIND INTEREST
Bankers say there are many reasons why Argentina arguably is the most attractive site for expansion in Latin America.

Restructuring or streamlining of the banking industry as a consequence of stricter solvency requirements introduced by the central bank in 1994, followed by the flight of deposits during the Tequila effect (the backlash from Mexican devaluation which plunged Argentina into recession) has meant local banks have sought to strengthen their capital base. Barbosa says because of this Argentine banks have looked for foreign partners.

Carlos Perez, manager of the research department at Banco Quilmes, says this "restructuring is a natural offensive process." Canada's Bank of Nova Scotia took a 25 percent stake in Quilmes last year. "This kind of incorporation (of foreign banks) will continue," says Perez.

The main interest is the large potential for growth in banking services. Argentina's domestic savings rate is just 18 percent of gross domestic product, much lower than that of neighbouring Chile which has a rate of 28 percent of GDP.
"Some 80 percent of the population is outside of the banking system, so there is a big development to take part in," says Barbosa.
SAVINGS SET TO RISE WITH PENSION INCENTIVE

With the economy emerging from recession and with more structural reforms in the pipeline, savings are set to rise. And most importantly, the introduction of a private pension system in 1994 is likely to make saving increasingly popular.
The private pension industry already manages $4.0 billion and is projected to capitalise some $20 billion by 2000. Foreign firms already have stakes in most of the large funds.
Reca says one of the biggest reasons Merrill decided to trade directly on the stock exchange is because of the existence of institutional investors.
Deutsche Morgan Grenfell announced last month it is consolidating its position in Argentina, something it put down to the development and growing sophistication of the markets.

"The sustained growth of domestic institutional investors, the consolidation of capital investments by local firms and culmination of state reforms are the critical factors contributing to making Argentina one of the most attractive places in the region," Deutsche said in a statement.
A natural conduit for overseas banks has been the ongoing privatisation process of Argentine state assets. Oil company YPF and many national utilities have already been sold.

But the anticipated "super privatisations" of state-owned Banco Nacion (Argentina's largest bank) and Banco de la Provincia de Buenos Aires remains for a second stage, promising to attract more foreign money, says Perez.
Furthermore, the anticipated privatisation of provincial banks is attracting interest from overseas banks, mainly U.S., says Barbosa.
Apart from that, the increasing attractions of investing in Argentine assets as the economy jumps back into growth is a reason for foreign banks to be here.
The net inflow of foreign capital to Argentine assets hit a record high of $14.1 billion in September.
Industry sources say coming to Argentina is also advantageous because if offers access to the Mercosur customs union between Brazil, Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay.
